title: Classification of Plants
status: draft: written 18 Nov 2026 offline for Grade 5 Science and Technology; not yet checked by a CBC Science and Technology teacher; not loaded by the live tutor
notes: Bring real flowers: a hibiscus or a bean flower that can be cut open, a maize tassel and silk, a fern and a moss from a damp wall, a cypress cone. The child cuts a flower open with a razor held by the teacher and finds each part with a hand lens.

skills.key_step: The child decides by whether a plant makes flowers and seeds in fruits at some time in its life, not by whether it has a bright flower today.

floor.question: Name one way a plant makes new plants.

representations: a maize tassel, a bean flower, a fern and a moss
pictures of a cypress cone and a mango flower
steps: Ask: does this plant ever make flowers?
Look for small green flowers too (maize, grass).
Ferns and mosses never flower: they make spores.
Cypress and pine make cones, not flowers.
contexts: a cypress hedge round the school

board.do: Draw a maize plant with a tassel and a fern.
Point at the tassel.
Wait for the child to decide.
Write "flowering" under the maize.
Ask whether the fern will ever make a flower.

misconceptions.ask: What is the tassel on top of a maize plant?
misconceptions.repair: Small green or yellow flowers are still flowers.

misconceptions.ask: What does a cypress tree make: flowers or cones?
misconceptions.repair: Cypress and pine make cones; they are non-flowering.

misconceptions.ask: Have you seen a fern make a flower or a seed?
misconceptions.repair: Ferns and mosses reproduce by spores and never flower.

misconceptions.ask: Will this kale plant make flowers later?
misconceptions.repair: Decide by the whole life of the plant, not one week.

checks.question: Is a fern a flowering or a non-flowering plant?
A bean plant has no flowers this week. Is it a non-flowering plant?
checks.answer: No: beans flower and make pods; it is a flowering plant

skills.key_step: The child names the sepal, petal, stamen (anther and filament) and pistil (stigma, style, ovary) on a real flower, from the outside in.

floor.prerequisite: Knows the roots, stem and leaves of a plant.
floor.question: Which part of a plant makes food?

representations: a hibiscus or bean flower cut open
a labelled drawing of a half flower
cards with part names to place on the drawing
steps: Outside: sepals (green, protect the bud).
Next: petals (bright).
Then the stamens: anther on a filament.
Middle: the pistil: stigma on top, style, ovary at the bottom.

board.do: Draw a half flower with sepals, petals, stamens and a pistil.
Point at the sticky top of the middle part.
Wait for the child to name the stigma.
Ask the child to label the anther and the ovary.

misconceptions.ask: Which parts cover the bud before it opens?
misconceptions.repair: The green parts under the flower are sepals; the bright parts are petals.

listen_for: the middle one is the stamen
misconceptions.ask: Which part has pollen on its tip?
misconceptions.repair: Stamens carry pollen; the pistil is in the middle.

listen_for: the stigma is on the stamen
misconceptions.ask: Is the sticky top in the middle or on the thin stalks?
misconceptions.repair: The stigma tops the pistil; the anther tops the stamen.

misconceptions.ask: Has this flower been pollinated yet?
misconceptions.repair: In a fresh flower it is the ovary; it becomes the fruit later.

checks.question: Name the part of the flower that holds the pollen.
Name the three parts of the pistil.

skills.key_step: The child gives each part its job: sepals protect the bud, petals and nectar draw insects, anthers make pollen, the stigma receives pollen, the ovary holds the ovules that become seeds.

floor.prerequisite: Can name the parts of a flower.
floor.question: Name the part at the bottom of the pistil.

representations: a bee at a flower in the school garden
a labelled half flower with jobs written beside it
a matching game: part and job
steps: Sepals: protect the bud.
Petals and nectar: draw insects.
Anther: makes pollen; stigma: receives it.
Ovary: holds ovules, which become seeds.

board.do: Draw a bee on a flower with pollen on its legs.
Point at the pollen.
board.say: Where did the pollen come from, and where is it going?

board.do: Wait for anther and stigma.
Write the job beside each part.

misconceptions.ask: Which parts are bright and seen from far?
misconceptions.repair: Petals attract insects; sepals protect the bud.

misconceptions.ask: Does pollen grow into a plant when planted?
misconceptions.repair: Pollen is not a seed; it must reach a stigma first.

misconceptions.ask: Where do you see the yellow dust: on the stamens or the pistil?
misconceptions.repair: The anther makes pollen; the ovary holds the ovules.

misconceptions.ask: Who drinks the nectar?
misconceptions.repair: Nectar draws insects that carry pollen.

checks.question: What is the job of the stigma?
Why do many flowers have bright petals and nectar?
checks.answer: to attract insects that carry pollen

skills.key_step: The child tells the order: pollen moves from an anther to a stigma (pollination), the ovary swells into the fruit, the ovules become seeds, and the petals fall.

floor.prerequisite: Knows the jobs of the flower parts.
floor.question: Which part receives pollen?

representations: a bean flower, a young pod and a full pod side by side
a flow chart with four boxes
a story of a bee visiting two flowers
steps: Pollination: pollen carried by insects or wind to a stigma.
The ovary starts to swell.
The petals dry and fall.
The ovary becomes the fruit; ovules become seeds.
contexts: a tomato plant in a kitchen garden
maize silk catching pollen from the tassel

board.do: Draw four boxes in a row: flower, pollination, swelling ovary, fruit.
Point at the second box.
Wait for insects or wind.
Ask the child to draw what is in the last box.
Label the fruit and the seeds.

misconceptions.ask: Where on the mango tree do the mangoes appear: where the flowers were?
misconceptions.repair: Fruits grow from flowers.

misconceptions.ask: Is the bee carrying pollen or seeds?
misconceptions.repair: Pollination carries pollen; dispersal spreads seeds later.

misconceptions.ask: What happens if no pollen reaches the stigma?
misconceptions.repair: Without pollination, most flowers make no fruit.

listen_for: the petals turn into the fruit
misconceptions.ask: What happened to the petals of the bean flower after a week?
misconceptions.repair: Petals fall; the ovary becomes the fruit.

checks.question: Which part of the flower becomes the fruit?
Put in order: fruit forms, pollen lands on stigma, ovary swells.
checks.answer: pollen lands on stigma, ovary swells, fruit forms

skills.key_step: The child links flowers with seeds and fruits people eat, with food for bees and other insects, with honey, and with new plants, not only with beauty.

floor.prerequisite: Knows a flower becomes a fruit with seeds.
floor.question: Which part of a flower becomes the fruit?

representations: a plate of foods that came from flowers (beans, maize, mango)
a chart: flower, what it gives
steps: Flowers make fruits and seeds we eat.
Seeds grow into new plants.
Nectar and pollen feed bees, which make honey.
Flowers are also sold and used for decoration.

board.do: Draw a plate of githeri.
Point at the beans and maize.
board.say: Where did these come from on the plant?

board.do: Wait for the child to say flowers.
Write "flower -> fruit/seed -> food".

misconceptions.ask: What does a bean flower turn into?
misconceptions.repair: Flowers give us fruits and seeds, not only beauty.

listen_for: kill the bees on the flowers
misconceptions.ask: What would happen to the mangoes if all the bees were killed?
misconceptions.repair: Insects on flowers carry pollen and help make fruit.

listen_for: maize does not come from a flower
misconceptions.ask: What was on the maize plant before the cob filled?
misconceptions.repair: Grain, beans and fruits all come from flowers.

misconceptions.ask: What does the silk catch?
misconceptions.repair: No flowers, no pollination, no grain.

checks.question: Give two ways flowers are important in nature.
checks.answer: any two: they make fruits and seeds, feed bees and insects, give new plants

checks.question: Why do farmers keep bees near their crops?
checks.answer: bees pollinate the flowers so more fruits and seeds form
